Branquinha attains a maximum recorded total length of 27 centimeters [Li = 27 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-bodied members of the Curimatidae family inhabiting the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Field surveys indicate that individuals approach this asymptotic length only after several years of growth, with sexually immature fish considerably smaller. The total length at puberty has been determined to be 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters], marking the point at which gonadal recrudescence first becomes detectable. This relatively modest size at maturation suggests that reproductive activity commences well before the cessation of somatic expansion, a pattern observed in many characiform species with indeterminate growth. Comparative data from related curimatids show that the length at first maturation often correlates with local productivity regimes, with populations in nutrient-rich floodplains reaching pubertal size more rapidly than those in oligotrophic clearwater tributaries. In Branquinha specifically, the transition from juvenile to reproductive life stages appears to coincide with the occupation of seasonally inundated habitats, where prey availability and thermal conditions support both continued somatic growth and initial gamete production.

Neonatal body mass in this species is remarkably low, with newly emerged larvae weighing 0.0072 grams [Wwb = 0.0072 grams]. This minute wet weight at birth reflects the small diameter of the fertilised eggs, which are typical of pelagic-spawning characiforms that produce numerous, poorly provisioned oocytes. The yolk-sac larva absorbs its endogenous reserves within the first week post-hatching, initiating exogenous feeding soon after mouth opening. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the age at birth—defined as the moment of chorion rupture—was recorded as 8 days [ab = 8 days]. This incubation period is consistent with values reported for other Potamorhina species, although slight variation occurs depending on dissolved oxygen levels and parental microhabitat selection in the wild. The rapid transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition places a premium on the timely availability of small zooplanktonic prey, particularly rotifers and early-stage copepod nauplii, in the surrounding water column during the first days of exogenous feeding.

The wet weight at puberty, measured at the onset of gonadal maturation in reproductively active individuals, is 34.82 grams [Wwp = 34.82 grams]. This mass threshold represents an approximately 4800-fold increase over the mass at hatching, highlighting the substantial somatic investment required before the onset of reproductive competence. In field-captured specimens, individuals below this mass routinely display immature gonadal tissue, whereas those exceeding it typically exhibit developing oocytes or spermatogenic activity. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Branquinha is 271 grams [Wwi = 271 grams], a value that corresponds closely with the maximum total length of 27 centimeters. This asymptotic mass appears to be relatively invariant across the species' geographic range, suggesting strong phylogenetic or biomechanical constraints on final body size. Compared with sympatric detritivorous characiforms, Branquinha achieves a slightly lower ultimate mass than the larger Prochilodus species but exceeds that of most small-bodied Curimata, occupying an intermediate trophic and size niche within the neotropical fish assemblage.

Reproductive output was estimated from gravid females collected during the peak spawning season. Each female was found to carry approximately 271 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 271 eggs per spawning event], a fecundity that is intermediate for a curimatid of this body size. The daily maximum reproduction rate, when integrated over the breeding season, reflects the product of this clutch size and the observed spawning interval. At the prevailing water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], females were recorded producing roughly 2.6 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 2.6 spawning events per year]. This rate of reproductive events indicates a protracted spawning season, with individual females capable of multiple clutches during the annual flood pulse when hydrological connectivity and food availability peak. The combination of modest batch fecundity and moderate annual spawning frequency results in a lifetime reproductive output that is highly dependent on adult survival across successive breeding seasons, a life-history strategy typical of iteroparous neotropical freshwater teleosts.

Maximum lifespan in Branquinha has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and otolith annulus analyses, with the oldest documented individual reaching approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] in the wild at a temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]. This longevity is notable for a species of its adult body mass, as many similarly sized neotropical characiforms senesce after 5 to 8 years. The extended lifespan likely reflects a combination of low natural predation pressure in deep-channel habitats and a relatively slow metabolic pace, sustained by a detritivorous feeding strategy that avoids the high energetic costs of piscivory. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the age at birth was consistently observed at 8 days [ab = 8 days], a developmental period that, when projected against the full lifespan, represents an extremely brief fraction of the total life cycle. The life history of Branquinha thus combines rapid early ontogeny with a prolonged reproductive window, allowing individuals to exploit interannual variation in floodplain productivity and ensuring population persistence across decades of variable environmental conditions.
